A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPELA research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v2 reports original SPELA training, few-shot, transfer-learning, and ablation results in the main text and Appendix B.

after.justification: v3 reports original MLP and CNN experiments, GPU-memory measurements, transfer-learning results, and sensitivity analyses, including appendix results.

M1.justification: The optimized MLP procedure called SPELA(O) in v2 is retained as SPELA. However, v3 introduces a substantial CNN extension using kernel-specific class groups, auxiliary MLPs, local updates, and class-score voting (Section 3.5 and Algorithm 2). It also introduces cross-entropy training variants alongside cosine-loss training.

E1.justification: Transfer-learning coverage expands from Aircraft 100, CIFAR 10, Flowers 102, and Pets 37 to include CIFAR 100 and Food 101. Food 101 is a new dataset/domain; CIFAR 100 already appeared in v2's MLP experiments. The CNN evaluations use CIFAR 10, CIFAR 100, and SVHN 10, all already represented in v2.

E2.justification: v3 adds an actual Forward-Forward result to Table 3, whereas v2 discussed FF without including its accuracy there. BP results also fill previously absent comparisons on KMNIST and Fashion MNIST in Table 3 and SVHN in Table 7. FA, DRTP, and PEPITA remain comparators.

E3.justification: v3 introduces explicit A/B MLP configurations with different training budgets and settings. Transfer experiments change from 50 epochs at learning rate 0.001 with multilayer heads and varying test percentages to 200 epochs at 0.1 with class-sized or fivefold heads and a fixed test set. New protocols measure memory across depths and batch sizes and evaluate CNN configurations.

E4.justification: v3 adds depth, learning-rate, and CNN-channel sensitivity studies; expands the output-width analysis; and adds angular loss, normalized Euclidean distance, and uniformly random embeddings to the ablations. Conversely, v2's dedicated few-shot/few-epoch analysis and weight-distribution/QQ-plot analyses are removed, rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Five-run mean and standard-deviation reporting remains the prevailing practice. v3 additionally specifies five runs for the ablations in Tables 5 and 16, where v2's Table 6 did not state a run count. This is additional documentation, not evidence that run counts increased.

E6.justification: The numerical evidence is extensively replaced and expanded. For example, v2 Table 3 reports 96.66%, 93.63%, and 89.77% for SPELA(O), while v3 reports 94.49%, 76.36%, and 85.00% for SPELA_B under revised architecture and training settings. These are not directly comparable performance declines. Transfer tables are replaced, and CNN, memory, depth, and sensitivity results are added.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.4 adds an explicit chain-rule derivation of normalized cosine-loss gradients and local weight/bias updates, beyond v2's gradient-update pseudocode. The complexity orders for the retained optimized method and the appendix's embedding-energy definition remain essentially unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the claimed advantage from less data, computing, storage, and power to less memory. Rapid few-shot/few-epoch learning is dropped as a principal contribution. CNN training and claimed performance equivalence to backpropagation become central contributions in the abstract, introduction, and discussion.

C2.justification: The interpretation shifts from rapid learning and extreme trained weights toward memory scaling and classifier-width tradeoffs. v3 explains why normalization makes Euclidean distance more suitable, acknowledges slightly higher model memory from classifier heads, and identifies CNN group-consistency restrictions and missing biological spiking behavior. These materially expand the mechanisms and applicability boundaries discussed.

D1.justification: New Appendix C and Tables 19–23 systematically document architectures, batch sizes, optimizers, initialization, dropout, bias, activations, learning-rate schedules, and training budgets, plus the NVIDIA RTX 4500 Ada GPU. v2 supplied much sparser settings. v3 also expands the electron-simulation stopping description and identifies PyTorch Hub as the pretrained ResNet50 source.

R1.justification: v3 adds Li et al. (2025) on NoProp, Cer et al. (2018) for angular similarity, and Liao et al. (2016) in the CNN discussion. The broader positioning against backpropagation alternatives, including identifying PEPITA as the closest approach, remains substantially intact.

P1.justification: The main five-section organization and considerable existing prose remain. v3 copyedits the language, standardizes SPELA(O) to SPELA, condenses the training description, moves embedding construction into Appendix A.1, changes ablation headings, and collects experimental settings in Appendix C. These are bounded editorial and organizational revisions alongside the larger scientific changes.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with an added loss panel and training-accuracy curves; Figure 3 incorporates a CNN schematic. New width, memory, and learning-rate plots replace or supplement earlier displays. Transfer plots are reorganized across Figures 6 and 8 with additional curves and changed axes. Comparison tables expand structurally, numerous analysis/settings tables appear, and the few-shot and QQ displays disappear.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central efficiency argument by adding measured memory scaling where v2 relied mainly on restricted theoretical estimates. Appendix C greatly improves experimental transparency, while a fixed test set and expanded sensitivity analyses make evaluation more informative. These gains outweigh new local errors, including the omitted gradient factor in Section 3.4 and Section 4.5's attribution of PEPITA's 56.33% score to SPELA. Those errors and the broad CNN-equivalence claim still require correction.
